A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GEMS research, despite a changed title and document format. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original GEMS and baseline experiments across three datasets and settings in Tables 1–3, with additional evaluations and ablations in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original classical-baseline comparisons, proprietary-LLM evaluations, error analysis, and ensemble results.

M1.justification: The graph construction, encoders, decoder, losses, and LLM-to-GNN projection remain unchanged. v2 adds an inference variant that averages predicted probabilities from 11 differently initialized GEMS models (Section 6, Table 6).

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate OpinionQA, Twin-2K, and Dunning–Kruger responses under missing-response, new-individual, and new-question settings. The added comparisons and analyses use this existing coverage; the change from discrete-choice to close-ended terminology does not introduce a different task.

E2.justification: v2 adds XGBoost in Settings 1–2 and matrix factorization in Setting 1 across all three datasets (Table 5). It also adds GPT-5-Mini, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3 Flash prompting comparisons on OpinionQA (Table 9). Qwen2.5-7B, evaluated in v1 Table 5, is removed from the corresponding extended comparison in v2 Table 8.

E3.justification: v2 introduces paired-correctness evaluation of the best GEMS and LLM methods across three OpinionQA settings, plus an 11-model ensemble evaluation. The existing individual-level and question-level splits, accuracy metric, edge masking, and main training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds error-overlap analysis (Table 4), classical controls examining the contribution of graph structure (Table 5), and an ensemble study testing whether inexpensive repeated training improves accuracy (Table 6). The earlier LoRA-capacity, hidden-layer, and projection-pair ablations are retained in Appendix F.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies 11 different model initializations for the ensemble. This is ensemble construction, not an increase in uncertainty-estimation runs for the existing results. Tables 1–3 retain the same three-split mean-and-standard-deviation reporting, and the LoRA ablation remains explicitly single-seed.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds classical-baseline, proprietary-model, error-overlap, and ensemble results. For example, Gemini 3 Flash reaches 52.78% with 8-shot Agentic CoT on OpinionQA Setting 1, while the new GEMS ensemble reaches 51.65% in Setting 3 versus 50.13% for the retained single-model result. Extended-table values are also corrected: Mistral-7B zero-shot accuracy changes from 35.60 in v1 Table 5 to 34.63 in v2 Table 8, matching Table 1; this does not establish a same-setting performance change from rerunning experiments.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, mathematical objectives, and encoder/decoder equations are retained. Changes such as replacing the GraphSAGE root-transformation symbol with the self-transformation symbol are not substantive mathematical revisions. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims of competitive accuracy, much smaller models, efficiency, and transparency remain. v1's explicit headline claim of greater interpretability is narrowed in v2 to insights obtained from inspecting embeddings, rather than retained as a principal comparative advantage.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning greater GEMS–LLM error complementarity on unseen questions, message-passing advantages over classical baselines, affordable ensembling, and diminishing returns from larger prompted LLMs. Most existing limitations remain. However, the Setting 3 discussion drops v1's explicit acknowledgment that GEMS does not outperform few-shot fine-tuning.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new baselines' per-question one-hot inputs and factorization objective, and specifies probability averaging for the ensemble. Appendix C.3 corrects the stated expected-performance subgroup count from 11 to 10 while retaining the listed bins. Existing GEMS hyperparameters, hardware information, prompts, and code-access information are largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including Bianchi et al. and Zhou et al. on open-ended simulation and Lakshminarayanan et al. on ensembles, while removing works including Tang et al. and the Qwen2.5 report. Its positioning between LLM simulation, graph recommendation, and classical discrete-choice modeling remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, extensively rewrites the abstract and introduction, replaces much discrete-choice terminology with close-ended simulation, and restructures the narrative. Related work moves before the problem definition, while limitations and ethical considerations move from Appendix A into main-text Sections 8–9.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, substantially reflowing equations, tables, and prompt examples. v2 adds Tables 4–6 and 9 and restructures the extended LLM table. The original three-panel compute figure is retained as appendix Figure 4, alongside a revised Setting 1 display in main-text Figure 3.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important comparative gap in v1 by adding learned classical baselines, allowing readers to assess whether graph modeling offers value beyond simpler non-language methods. Four proprietary-LLM comparisons, error-overlap analysis, and measured ensemble gains substantially strengthen the evidence supporting the paper's central argument; corrected extended-table scores also improve consistency. The added comparisons still provide limited uncertainty and implementation detail, and the Setting 3 discussion is less explicit about trailing fine-tuning, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.
